key_terms.meaning: A loop with no loop inside it in a planar circuit; a mesh current circulates round it. b − n + 1 meshes.
R<sub>kk</sub> = all resistance in mesh k; R<sub>kj</sub> = −(resistance shared by meshes k and j) with clockwise currents.
Two meshes sharing a current source: one KVL round the outer path plus the source's current constraint.
Voltage of a node above the reference node (0 V); n − 1 unknowns for n nodes.
Two non-reference nodes joined by a voltage source: one KCL for the pair plus v<sub>+</sub> − v<sub>−</sub> = V<sub>s</sub>.
Homogeneity (scaling) plus additivity; y = Σ a<sub>k</sub>x<sub>k</sub> over the independent sources.
Total response = sum of single-source responses; off voltage source = short, off current source = open; dependent sources stay; power does not superpose.
V<sub>th</sub> = open-circuit voltage in series with R<sub>th</sub> = resistance with independent sources off.
I<sub>N</sub> = short-circuit current in parallel with R<sub>N</sub> = R<sub>th</sub>; R<sub>th</sub> = V<sub>oc</sub>/I<sub>sc</sub>.
Independent sources off, dependent kept, apply V<sub>t</sub>, find I<sub>t</sub>: R<sub>th</sub> = V<sub>t</sub>/I<sub>t</sub>.
R<sub>L</sub> = R<sub>th</sub>; P<sub>max</sub> = V<sub>th</sub>²/(4R<sub>th</sub>); equivalent-circuit efficiency 50 %.
One source in a linear bilateral network: swapping source and ammeter leaves the reading unchanged.
Σ v<sub>k</sub>i<sub>k</sub> = 0 over all branches (passive convention) for any network obeying KCL and KVL.
Branch Z with current I changed by ΔZ: the changes are the currents of a source V<sub>c</sub> = IΔZ, opposing I, acting alone in the changed network.
Z = R + jX (Z<sub>L</sub> = jωL, Z<sub>C</sub> = −j/(ωC)); Y = 1/Z in siemens.
Z<sub>L</sub> = Z<sub>th</sub>* gives P<sub>max</sub> = |V<sub>th</sub>|²/(4R<sub>th</sub>) with RMS phasors; a resistor-only load is best at R<sub>L</sub> = |Z<sub>th</sub>|.

takeaways: Mesh analysis writes one KVL per window with clockwise mesh currents; a current source on a shared branch makes a supermesh, and a dependent source is written in mesh currents.
Nodal analysis writes one KCL per non-reference node; a voltage source between two such nodes makes a supernode, and a source to the reference simply fixes a node voltage.
Superposition adds voltages and currents, one independent source at a time, with dependent sources kept on in every run; power is found once, from the total.
Any linear two-terminal network is V<sub>th</sub> behind R<sub>th</sub>, or I<sub>N</sub> across R<sub>th</sub>; with dependent sources use V<sub>oc</sub>/I<sub>sc</sub> or a test source.
A load takes the most power at R<sub>L</sub> = R<sub>th</sub>, V<sub>th</sub>²/(4R<sub>th</sub>), but at no more than 50 % efficiency, so power systems avoid it.
Reciprocity and Tellegen's theorem are quick checks; Millman's theorem solves parallel source branches in one line.
The compensation theorem gives the effect of a changed element or an inserted meter from one small source, V<sub>c</sub> = IΔZ.
With phasors and impedances every method holds in AC; different frequencies are solved separately, and maximum power needs Z<sub>L</sub> = Z<sub>th</sub>*.
bank_note: Long answers in this unit are worked circuits: draw and label the circuit, state the law or theorem, write the equations, solve with units, and close with a check (KCL at a node, a power balance, or the same answer by a second method). Most syllabi ask for these methods with dependent sources and for both DC and AC circuits, and ask for the statement and proof of each theorem along with a numerical example.

bank.q: Explain the steps of mesh analysis and how the mesh equations of a planar network are written in matrix form by inspection. Apply them to this ladder: a 20 V source (+ at the top) in the left branch; resistors of 2 Ω, 6 Ω and 4 Ω along the top from left to right; 4 Ω and 3 Ω vertical resistors from the two inner top junctions to the bottom wire; and a 10 V source (+ at the top) in the right branch. Find the three mesh currents and check the power balance.
outline: Planar circuit, meshes = b − n + 1, clockwise mesh currents
Self-resistance on the diagonal, minus mutual resistance off it, source rises on the right
Solve: i₁ = 4 A, i₂ = 1 A, i₃ = −1 A
Branch currents and a 90 W power balance
answer: Method. (1) Check the circuit is planar and count meshes: b − n + 1. (2) Draw a clockwise current in each mesh. (3) In mesh k, add the drops: R × ik for its own resistors and R(ik − ij) for a resistor shared with mesh j; equate to the net source rise met when walking clockwise. (4) Solve. (5) Find branch currents as mesh currents or their differences, and check.

By inspection. The equations form R i = v. Rkk (self-resistance) is the total resistance round mesh k; Rkj is minus the resistance shared by meshes k and j; vk is the sum of source rises in mesh k in the clockwise direction. With independent sources only the matrix is symmetric.

The ladder. Branches: two sources and five resistors, b = 7. Nodes: the bottom wire and four top junctions, n = 5. Meshes: 7 − 5 + 1 = 3. Mesh 1 holds the 20 V source, the 2 Ω and the 4 Ω (shared with mesh 2); mesh 2 holds the 4 Ω, the 6 Ω and the 3 Ω (shared with mesh 3); mesh 3 holds the 3 Ω, the top 4 Ω and the 10 V source.

answer.text: Matrix by inspection. R₁₁ = 2 + 4 = 6 Ω, R₂₂ = 4 + 6 + 3 = 13 Ω, R₃₃ = 3 + 4 = 7 Ω, R₁₂ = −4 Ω, R₂₃ = −3 Ω, R₁₃ = 0. Walking clockwise, mesh 1 goes up through the 20 V source (− to +): v₁ = +20 V. Mesh 3 goes down through the 10 V source (+ to −), a drop: v₃ = −10 V.
Solve. From row 1, i₁ = (20 + 4i₂)/6. From row 3, i₃ = (−10 + 3i₂)/7. Put both into row 2 and multiply by 42:

answer: Branch currents. 2 Ω: 4 A. 4 Ω (vertical): i₁ − i₂ = 3 A downward. 6 Ω: 1 A. 3 Ω: i₂ − i₃ = 1 − (−1) = 2 A downward. Top 4 Ω and the 10 V source: i₃ = −1 A, that is 1 A flowing anticlockwise in mesh 3, which is upward through the 10 V source.

answer.text: Power balance.

answer: Checks. Row 2 with the answers: −4(4) + 13(1) − 3(−1) = −16 + 13 + 3 = 0. The matrix is symmetric, as it must be with independent sources only. Both sources deliver power: the 10 V source is driven by the larger 20 V source through the ladder.
Answer. i₁ = 4 A, i₂ = 1 A, i₃ = −1 A; 90 W delivered and absorbed.

bank.q: State the superposition theorem and explain why it holds for linear circuits. Use it for this circuit: a 10 V source in series with 2 Ω feeds node a; node a has 10 Ω to the reference and 5 Ω to node b; node b has 10 Ω to the reference and a 2 A source driving current from the reference into b. Find the current in the 5 Ω, its power, and explain why the power is not the sum of the two partial powers.
outline: Statement; linear equations, response = Σ a<sub>k</sub>x<sub>k</sub>
Run 1: 2 A opened, I′ = 0.5 A from a to b
Run 2: 10 V shorted, I″ = 1.2 A from b to a
Total 0.7 A from b to a; nodal check
Power 2.45 W, not 8.45 W; cross term −6 W
answer: Statement. In a linear circuit with several independent sources, any voltage or current equals the algebraic sum of the voltages or currents produced by each independent source acting alone, with every other independent source switched off (voltage sources shorted, current sources opened) and every dependent source left in place.

Why it holds. Nodal (or mesh) analysis of a linear circuit gives simultaneous equations with constant coefficients, and the source values appear only on the right side. The solution is therefore y = a₁x₁ + a₂x₂ + … : a weighted sum of the source values. Setting all but x₁ to zero gives the term a₁x₁, and so on; the terms add up to y.
Reference direction. Take the current I in the 5 Ω as positive from a to b.

Run 1: 10 V alone (2 A source opened). Node b now has only the 10 Ω to the reference, so the 5 Ω and that 10 Ω are in series (15 Ω), in parallel with the 10 Ω at node a: 15 × 10/25 = 6 Ω. The source sees 2 + 6 = 8 Ω and supplies 10/8 = 1.25 A. Va′ = 10 − 1.25 × 2 = 7.5 V. I′ = 7.5/15 = 0.5 A from a to b (Vb′ = 5 V).

Run 2: 2 A alone (10 V source shorted). The 2 Ω now runs from a to the reference, in parallel with the 10 Ω: 2 × 10/12 = 1.667 Ω. Seen from b: 10 Ω in parallel with (5 + 1.667) = 6.667 Ω, which is 10 × 6.667/16.667 = 4 Ω. Vb″ = 2 × 4 = 8 V. The current from b through the 5 Ω towards a is 8/6.667 = 1.2 A, so I″ = −1.2 A (Va″ = 1.2 × 1.667 = 2 V).

answer.text: Add.

answer: Result. I = 0.5 − 1.2 = −0.7 A: 0.7 A flows from b to a.

answer.text: Check by nodal analysis with both sources on (Va = 9.5 V, Vb = 13 V):
Power. P = I²R = 0.7² × 5 = 2.45 W. The partial powers add to 1.25 + 7.2 = 8.45 W, which is wrong. Because P is a square:

answer: The cross term 2I′I″R = −6 W is what the sum of partial powers leaves out; here the two runs push current in opposite directions, so the true power is much smaller than either run suggests.
Limits. Superposition needs linear elements and is used only for voltages and currents. Dependent sources are never switched off, and power is computed once from the total.

bank.q: State Thevenin's and Norton's theorems and give the relations between their parameters. A 12 V source (no internal resistance, + at A) feeds a bridge: 3 Ω from A to C, 6 Ω from C to B, 6 Ω from A to D and 3 Ω from D to B. A galvanometer of 8 Ω is connected between C and D. Find the galvanometer current with Thevenin's theorem, then check it with Norton's theorem and by nodal analysis.
outline: Statements and R<sub>N</sub> = R<sub>th</sub>, I<sub>N</sub> = V<sub>th</sub>/R<sub>th</sub>
Remove the galvanometer: V<sub>C</sub> = 8 V, V<sub>D</sub> = 4 V, V<sub>th</sub> = 4 V
Source shorted: R<sub>th</sub> = 3 ∥ 6 + 6 ∥ 3 = 4 Ω
I<sub>g</sub> = 4/(4 + 8) = 0.333 A from C to D
Norton I<sub>N</sub> = 1 A gives the same; nodal check
answer: Thevenin's theorem. Any linear two-terminal network can be replaced at its terminals by a voltage source Vth, equal to the open-circuit voltage, in series with Rth, the resistance seen at the terminals with every independent source switched off (dependent sources kept).
Norton's theorem. The same network can be replaced by a current source IN, equal to the short-circuit current, in parallel with RN.
Relations. RN = Rth; IN = Vth/Rth; Vth = INRN; Rth = Voc/Isc.
Step 1: remove the load. The galvanometer is the load; take B as the reference (0 V), so A is at 12 V.

answer.text: Step 2: open-circuit voltage. With the galvanometer removed, each side of the bridge is a divider:
answer.pre:
V<sub>C</sub> = 12 × 6/(3 + 6) = 8 V
V<sub>D</sub> = 12 × 3/(6 + 3) = 4 V
V<sub>th</sub> = V<sub>C</sub> − V<sub>D</sub> = 4 V   (C positive)

answer: Step 3: Thevenin resistance. Short the 12 V source, which joins A to B. Seen from C: 3 Ω (to A) in parallel with 6 Ω (to B) = 2 Ω. Seen from D: 6 Ω in parallel with 3 Ω = 2 Ω. The two are in series between C and D: Rth = 2 + 2 = 4 Ω.
Step 4: galvanometer current. Ig = Vth/(Rth + Rg) = 4/(4 + 8) = 0.333 A, flowing from C to D through the galvanometer.
Norton check. IN = Vth/Rth = 4/4 = 1 A in parallel with 4 Ω. Current divider into the 8 Ω galvanometer: 1 × 4/(4 + 8) = 0.333 A. Same answer.

answer.text: Nodal check with the galvanometer in place (unknowns VC, VD; VA = 12 V):
answer.pre:
node C: (V<sub>C</sub> − 12)/3 + V<sub>C</sub>/6 + (V<sub>C</sub> − V<sub>D</sub>)/8 = 0
node D: (V<sub>D</sub> − 12)/6 + V<sub>D</sub>/3 + (V<sub>D</sub> − V<sub>C</sub>)/8 = 0
solution: V<sub>C</sub> = 7.333 V, V<sub>D</sub> = 4.667 V
I<sub>g</sub> = (7.333 − 4.667)/8 = 0.333 A   ✓

answer: Why Thevenin is quicker here. The nodal check needs two simultaneous equations; Thevenin needs two dividers and two parallel pairs, and it gives the current for any galvanometer at once: Ig = 4/(4 + Rg).
Balance. The bridge would be balanced (Vth = 0, no galvanometer current) if 3/6 = 6/3, that is if RACRDB = RCBRAD. Here 3 × 3 = 9 is not 6 × 6 = 36, so a current flows.
Answer. Vth = 4 V, Rth = 4 Ω, IN = 1 A; the galvanometer carries 0.333 A from C to D.

bank.q: State and prove the maximum power transfer theorem for a DC network. An 18 V source in series with 3 Ω has 6 Ω connected across its output, and 2 Ω runs from there to terminal a (terminal b is the bottom wire). Find the load that takes maximum power, the maximum power, the efficiency of the equivalent circuit, and the true efficiency of the network at that load. Tabulate the load power for loads of 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 Ω.
outline: Statement
P<sub>L</sub> = V<sub>th</sub>²R<sub>L</sub>/(R<sub>th</sub> + R<sub>L</sub>)², derivative, R<sub>L</sub> = R<sub>th</sub>, P<sub>max</sub> = V<sub>th</sub>²/(4R<sub>th</sub>)
V<sub>th</sub> = 12 V, R<sub>th</sub> = 4 Ω, P<sub>max</sub> = 9 W
Equivalent η = 50 %; network η = 9/54 = 16.7 %
Table showing the peak and the symmetry 2 × 8 = 16 = 4²
answer: Statement. A load resistance connected to a linear network takes the greatest power when it equals the network's Thevenin resistance, RL = Rth; the maximum power is Vth²/(4Rth).

answer.text: Proof. Replace the network by Vth in series with Rth. The load current is Vth/(Rth + RL), so
answer.pre:
P<sub>L</sub> = V<sub>th</sub>² R<sub>L</sub> / (R<sub>th</sub> + R<sub>L</sub>)²
dP<sub>L</sub>/dR<sub>L</sub> = V<sub>th</sub>² [(R<sub>th</sub> + R<sub>L</sub>)² − 2R<sub>L</sub>(R<sub>th</sub> + R<sub>L</sub>)] / (R<sub>th</sub> + R<sub>L</sub>)⁴
             = V<sub>th</sub>² (R<sub>th</sub> − R<sub>L</sub>) / (R<sub>th</sub> + R<sub>L</sub>)³

answer: Setting the derivative to zero gives R<sub>L</sub> = R<sub>th</sub>. The derivative is positive below R<sub>th</sub> and negative above it, so this is a maximum. Substituting: P<sub>max</sub> = V<sub>th</sub>²R<sub>th</sub>/(2R<sub>th</sub>)² = V<sub>th</sub>²/(4R<sub>th</sub>).
Thevenin equivalent of the given network. Open circuit: no current in the 2 Ω, so Vth = 18 × 6/(3 + 6) = 12 V. Source shorted: Rth = 2 + 3 × 6/9 = 2 + 2 = 4 Ω.
Maximum power. RL = 4 Ω; Pmax = 12²/(4 × 4) = 144/16 = 9 W. Check: I = 12/8 = 1.5 A and 1.5² × 4 = 9 W.

answer.text: Table from PL = 144RL/(4 + RL)² and η = RL/(4 + RL):

answer: The table is symmetric about the peak in the sense R₁R₂ = R<sub>th</sub>²: 1 Ω and 16 Ω both give 5.76 W, and 2 Ω and 8 Ω both give 8 W.
Efficiency of the equivalent circuit at the peak. VthI = 12 × 1.5 = 18 W supplied, 9 W in the load: 50 %.

True efficiency of the network. With the 4 Ω load, the load branch is 2 + 4 = 6 Ω, in parallel with the 6 Ω: 3 Ω. The 18 V source sees 3 + 3 = 6 Ω and supplies 3 A, that is 54 W. The load branch takes half of the 3 A, 1.5 A, so 9 W reaches the load: η = 9/54 = 16.7 %. The rest is lost in the 3 Ω (27 W), the 6 Ω (13.5 W) and the 2 Ω (4.5 W): 27 + 13.5 + 4.5 + 9 = 54 W.

Conclusion. The theorem gives the right load and the right load power, but the 50 % belongs to the equivalent circuit only. That is why maximum power transfer is used for weak signals and not for power supply.

bank.q: State and prove Tellegen's theorem. Verify it for this circuit: a 24 V source (+ at the top) in the left branch, 2 Ω in the top-left branch, 4 Ω in the shared middle branch, 2 Ω in the top-right branch, and a current-controlled voltage source of 2iₓ volts (+ at the top) in the right branch, where iₓ is the downward current in the 4 Ω. Then show that the theorem also holds with the voltages of this circuit and the currents of a second circuit with the same graph, in which the source is 12 V and the controlled source is replaced by a 2 Ω resistor.
outline: Statement with the passive sign convention
Proof from node potentials, KVL and KCL
Solve: i₁ = 6 A, i₂ = 3 A; branch powers −144, 72, 36, 18, 18 W
Second circuit: i₁′ = 3 A, i₂′ = 1.5 A
Σ v<sub>k</sub>i<sub>k</sub>′ = 0 and Σ v<sub>k</sub>′i<sub>k</sub> = 0; meaning and uses
answer: Statement. In any network with b branches whose voltages vk satisfy KVL and whose currents ik satisfy KCL, with each ik taken entering the + terminal of vk, Σ vkik = 0 over all branches.

Proof. (1) Because KVL holds, every node can be given a potential em so that a branch from node m to node n has vk = em − en. (2) Then Σ vkik = Σ (em − en)ik. (3) Group the terms by node: em is multiplied by the sum of the currents leaving node m. (4) By KCL each such sum is zero, so the whole sum is zero. Nothing about the elements was used, so the theorem holds for any elements, linear or not, and even when the voltages and the currents come from two different networks with the same graph.

answer.text: Solve the first circuit (clockwise mesh currents, iₓ = i₁ − i₂):
answer.pre:
mesh 1: 2i₁ + 4(i₁ − i₂) = 24          →  6i₁ − 4i₂ = 24
mesh 2: 2i₂ + 2(i₁ − i₂) + 4(i₂ − i₁) = 0  →  −2i₁ + 4i₂ = 0
i₁ = 2i₂,  8i₂ = 24  →  i₂ = 3 A,  i₁ = 6 A,  iₓ = 3 A,  2iₓ = 6 V

answer.text: Branch voltages, currents and powers (passive convention: a source whose current leaves its + terminal gets a negative product):

answer: The controlled source absorbs 18 W: the current enters its + terminal. The sum is zero, so the theorem holds, and it says the 144 W delivered by the 24 V source is exactly absorbed.

answer.text: Second circuit, same graph. Source 12 V and a 2 Ω resistor in place of the controlled source:

answer: Its branch currents, in the same order and directions: 3, 3, 1.5, 1.5, 1.5 A (the source term again taken as −3 A). Its branch voltages: 12, 6, 6, 3, 3 V.

answer.text: Cross sums.

answer: These cross sums are not powers of any real circuit; they are zero only because the voltages obey KVL and the currents obey KCL on the same graph. This is the form of the theorem used to prove reciprocity and to find sensitivities.

Uses. As a check after solving any circuit: a nonzero total means a sign slip or a missing branch. As a statement of conservation of energy for circuits that holds at every instant, for nonlinear and time-varying elements too.

bank.q: State and prove the compensation theorem. A 24 V source in series with 4 Ω feeds a 12 Ω resistor in parallel with a 6 Ω load. The load is changed to 9 Ω. Use the theorem to find the new load current and the changes in the other two currents, and check by direct solution.
outline: Statement: V<sub>c</sub> = IΔZ opposing I, sources off
Proof with the Thevenin equivalent: ΔI = −IΔZ/(Z<sub>th</sub> + Z + ΔZ)
Original: 3 A from the source, 2 A in the 6 Ω
V<sub>c</sub> = 6 V, ΔI = −0.5 A, new load current 1.5 A
12 Ω current +0.125 A, source current −0.375 A; direct check
answer: Statement. In a linear network, if the impedance Z of a branch carrying current I changes to Z + ΔZ, the change in every branch current equals the current produced, with all independent sources switched off, by a voltage source Vc = IΔZ placed in series with the changed branch and opposing I.

answer.text: Proof. Seen from the branch, the rest of the network is Vth behind Zth.
answer.pre:
I  = V<sub>th</sub>/(Z<sub>th</sub> + Z)
I′ = V<sub>th</sub>/(Z<sub>th</sub> + Z + ΔZ)
ΔI = I′ − I = −V<sub>th</sub>ΔZ / [(Z<sub>th</sub> + Z)(Z<sub>th</sub> + Z + ΔZ)] = −IΔZ/(Z<sub>th</sub> + Z + ΔZ)

answer: The last form is the current that a source IΔZ, opposing I, drives through the loop Z<sub>th</sub> + Z + ΔZ, which is the compensation network. Every other current responds linearly to the same change, so by superposition its change is the current this source drives in that branch.
Original circuit. 12 ∥ 6 = 4 Ω, so the source sees 4 + 4 = 8 Ω and supplies 24/8 = 3 A. Load: 3 × 12/18 = 2 A. 12 Ω: 1 A.
Compensating source. ΔR = 9 − 6 = 3 Ω, so Vc = IΔR = 2 × 3 = 6 V, opposing the load current.
Compensation network. Short the 24 V source. Vc drives the 9 Ω in series with 4 ∥ 12 = 3 Ω: ΔI = 6/(9 + 3) = 0.5 A against the load current. New load current 2 − 0.5 = 1.5 A.

Other branches. The 0.5 A splits between the 4 Ω and the 12 Ω: 0.5 × 12/16 = 0.375 A through the 4 Ω (the source current falls to 3 − 0.375 = 2.625 A) and 0.5 × 4/16 = 0.125 A through the 12 Ω (its current rises to 1 + 0.125 = 1.125 A).

answer.text: Direct check.

answer: Answer. The load current falls from 2 A to 1.5 A, the 12 Ω current rises to 1.125 A and the source current falls to 2.625 A.

bank.q: A planar circuit has three meshes, all currents clockwise. Mesh 1 has a 24 V source (+ at the top) in its left branch and 3 Ω in its top branch; a 4 Ω resistor is shared by meshes 1 and 2. Mesh 2 has 6 Ω in its top branch. The branch shared by meshes 2 and 3 holds only a 2 A current source pointing up. Mesh 3 has 2 Ω in its top branch and a plain wire as its right branch. Find the three mesh currents, the voltage across the current source, and check the power balance.
outline: Mesh 1 KVL: 7i₁ − 4i₂ = 24
Supermesh 2-3 round the outer path: −4i₁ + 10i₂ + 2i₃ = 0
Constraint i₃ − i₂ = 2 A
i₁ = 4 A, i₂ = 1 A, i₃ = 3 A
Source voltage 6 V; 108 W balance
answer: Plan. Mesh 1 contains no current source: ordinary KVL. The 2 A source sits on the branch shared by meshes 2 and 3, so these two form a supermesh with one KVL round their outer path and one constraint.
Mesh 1 (clockwise: up through the source, across the 3 Ω, down the 4 Ω): 3i₁ + 4(i₁ − i₂) = 24, so 7i₁ − 4i₂ = 24.

Supermesh (outer path of meshes 2 and 3: up the 4 Ω, across the 6 Ω and the 2 Ω, down the right wire, back along the bottom): 4(i₂ − i₁) + 6i₂ + 2i₃ = 0, so −4i₁ + 10i₂ + 2i₃ = 0. The current-source branch is left out.
Constraint. In the shared branch, clockwise i₂ flows down and clockwise i₃ flows up. The source points up, so i₃ − i₂ = 2 A.

answer.text: Solve.

answer: Branch currents. 3 Ω: 4 A. 4 Ω: i₁ − i₂ = 3 A downward. 6 Ω: 1 A. Current source branch: i₃ − i₂ = 2 A upward, as it must be. 2 Ω and the right wire: 3 A.

answer.text: Voltage across the current source. Write KVL round mesh 2 alone, with v the voltage of the top of the source above its bottom (a drop when mesh 2 walks down through it):
Power balance.

head: Element
Power (W)
rows: 2 A source, 6 V, current out of its + (top)

answer: Check the constraint sign. With the source reversed (pointing down) the constraint would be i₂ − i₃ = 2, a different circuit; always compare the arrow with each mesh current in that branch.
Answer. i₁ = 4 A, i₂ = 1 A, i₃ = 3 A; the current source has 6 V across it (top positive) and delivers 12 W.

bank.q: A circuit has a reference node and nodes 1, 2 and 3. Node 1 has 4 Ω to the reference and 8 Ω to node 3. A 6 V source joins node 2 (−) to node 1 (+). Node 2 has 2 Ω to node 3 and a voltage-controlled current source of 0.5vₓ amperes driving current from the reference into node 2, where vₓ = v₁ − v₃ is the voltage across the 8 Ω. Node 3 has 4 Ω to the reference and a 2 A source driving current from the reference into node 3. Find v₁, v₂, v₃, the current in the 6 V source, and check the power balance.
outline: Supernode of nodes 1 and 2 with v₁ − v₂ = 6
Supernode KCL with the controlled source written as 0.5(v₁ − v₃)
KCL at node 3
v₁ = 10 V, v₂ = 4 V, v₃ = 6 V
3 A through the 6 V source; 38 W balance
answer: Plan. The 6 V source joins two non-reference nodes, so nodes 1 and 2 form a supernode. Unknowns v₁, v₂, v₃; equations: supernode KCL, the constraint, and KCL at node 3.
Constraint (+ at node 1): v₁ − v₂ = 6.
Control variable. vₓ = v₁ − v₃, so the controlled source injects 0.5(v₁ − v₃) into node 2.

answer.text: Supernode KCL (currents leaving through resistors = currents entering from sources), then multiply by 8:
answer.pre:
v₁/4 + (v₁ − v₃)/8 + (v₂ − v₃)/2 = 0.5(v₁ − v₃)
2v₁ + (v₁ − v₃) + 4(v₂ − v₃) = 4(v₁ − v₃)
−v₁ + 4v₂ − v₃ = 0

answer.text: Node 3 KCL, multiplied by 8:
Solve with v₁ = v₂ + 6:

answer: Branch currents. 4 Ω at node 1: 10/4 = 2.5 A down. 8 Ω: (10 − 6)/8 = 0.5 A from node 1 to node 3. 2 Ω: (4 − 6)/2 = −1 A, that is 1 A from node 3 to node 2. 4 Ω at node 3: 6/4 = 1.5 A down. Controlled source: vₓ = 4 V, so it injects 2 A into node 2.

Current in the 6 V source. KCL at node 1 alone: 2.5 + 0.5 = 3 A leave through the resistors, so 3 A enter node 1 through the source, flowing from node 2 to node 1 (from − to + inside the source). Check at node 2: 1 A in from the 2 Ω plus 2 A from the controlled source = 3 A out into the source. ✓
Check node 3: in: 2 A (source) + 0.5 A (8 Ω) = 2.5 A; out: 1 A (to node 2) + 1.5 A (to reference) = 2.5 A. ✓

answer.text: Power balance.

answer: Answer. v₁ = 10 V, v₂ = 4 V, v₃ = 6 V; 3 A flows through the 6 V source from node 2 to node 1.

bank.q: A 12 V source (+ at the top) in series with 3 Ω feeds node x. A 1 A source drives current from the reference into x, and a 6 Ω resistor joins x to the reference; i₂ is the downward current in the 6 Ω. A current-controlled voltage source of 6i₂ volts joins x to terminal a, with its + at a. Terminal b is the reference. Find the Thevenin and Norton equivalents at a-b (i) from the open-circuit voltage and short-circuit current and (ii) with a test source. Find the current in a 6 Ω load and verify it by solving the circuit with the load in place. Also show how superposition splits V<sub>oc</sub> between the two independent sources.
outline: Open circuit: v<sub>x</sub> = 10 V, V<sub>oc</sub> = v<sub>x</sub> + 6i₂ = 20 V
Short circuit: v<sub>x</sub> = 0, I<sub>sc</sub> = 5 A
R<sub>th</sub> = 4 Ω; test source gives I<sub>t</sub> = V<sub>t</sub>/4
Wrong method (controlled source off) gives 2 Ω
6 Ω load: 2 A; direct check; V<sub>oc</sub> = 16 V + 4 V by superposition
answer: Relations used. Va − Vx = 6i₂ and i₂ = Vx/6, so Va = Vx + Vx = 2Vx whenever the 6 Ω carries Vx/6. The controlled source is in series with terminal a, so the current leaving a is the current through it.

answer.text: (i) Open circuit. No current leaves a, so KCL at x has three branches:
answer.pre:
(V<sub>x</sub> − 12)/3 + V<sub>x</sub>/6 = 1
2(V<sub>x</sub> − 12) + V<sub>x</sub> = 6   →   3V<sub>x</sub> = 30   →   V<sub>x</sub> = 10 V
i₂ = 10/6 = 1.667 A,  6i₂ = 10 V
V<sub>oc</sub> = V<sub>x</sub> + 6i₂ = 20 V   (a positive)

answer: (i) Short circuit. Join a to b: Va = 0 = 2Vx, so Vx = 0. Then the 6 Ω carries nothing, and all the current reaching x leaves through the controlled source to the short: Isc = 12/3 + 1 = 4 + 1 = 5 A.
Thevenin resistance. Rth = Voc/Isc = 20/5 = 4 Ω. Norton: IN = 5 A in parallel with 4 Ω.

answer.text: (ii) Test source. Short the 12 V source, open the 1 A source, keep the controlled source, and apply Vt at a. Still Va = 2Vx, so Vx = Vt/2. The test current It enters a, passes through the controlled source into x, and leaves through the 3 Ω and the 6 Ω:
answer.pre:
I<sub>t</sub> = V<sub>x</sub>/3 + V<sub>x</sub>/6 = V<sub>x</sub>/2 = V<sub>t</sub>/4
R<sub>th</sub> = V<sub>t</sub>/I<sub>t</sub> = 4 Ω   ✓

answer: Wrong method for comparison. Switching the controlled source off (replacing it by a short) leaves 3 ∥ 6 = 2 Ω, which is wrong: the controlled source doubles the voltage at a for every volt at x, which doubles the apparent resistance.
Load of 6 Ω. Thevenin: IL = 20/(4 + 6) = 2 A, load voltage 12 V. Norton: 5 × 4/(4 + 6) = 2 A. Same.

answer.text: Direct check with the load. The load current is Va/6 = 2Vx/6 = Vx/3, and it leaves x through the controlled source:
answer.pre:
(V<sub>x</sub> − 12)/3 + V<sub>x</sub>/6 + V<sub>x</sub>/3 = 1
2(V<sub>x</sub> − 12) + V<sub>x</sub> + 2V<sub>x</sub> = 6   →   5V<sub>x</sub> = 30   →   V<sub>x</sub> = 6 V
V<sub>a</sub> = 12 V,  I<sub>L</sub> = 12/6 = 2 A   ✓

answer.text: Superposition of Voc (controlled source kept in both runs):

answer: Power check with the 6 Ω load (Vx = 6 V): 12 V source supplies (12 − 6)/3 = 2 A, 24 W; 1 A source at 6 V, 6 W; controlled source: 2 A leaves its + terminal at a while it holds 6 V, so it delivers 12 W. Absorbed: 3 Ω 2² × 3 = 12 W, 6 Ω 1² × 6 = 6 W, load 2² × 6 = 24 W. 24 + 6 + 12 = 42 = 12 + 6 + 24. ✓
Answer. Vth = 20 V, Rth = 4 Ω, IN = 5 A; the 6 Ω load draws 2 A.

bank.q: (a) Two batteries, 15 V with 3 Ω internal resistance and 12 V with 2 Ω, are connected in parallel (both + to the top rail) across a 6 Ω load. Use Millman's theorem to find the load voltage and every current, and give the single equivalent source of the two batteries. (b) A ladder has branch 1, a 30 V source in series with 3 Ω, feeding node x; 6 Ω from x to the reference; 4 Ω from x to node y; 12 Ω from y to the reference; and branch 2, an ammeter in series with 2 Ω, from y to the reference. Find the ammeter reading, then swap the source and the ammeter and verify reciprocity.
outline: Battery currents 1.333 A and 0.5 A, load 1.833 A
Equivalent of the batteries: 13.2 V behind 1.2 Ω
Ladder forward: 2.222 A in branch 2
Swapped: 2.222 A in branch 1; conditions for reciprocity

answer.text: (a) Millman's theorem. Treat the load as a third branch with no source:

answer: Currents. 15 V battery: (15 − 11)/3 = 1.333 A out of its + terminal. 12 V battery: (12 − 11)/2 = 0.5 A out of its + terminal. Load: 11/6 = 1.833 A. Check: 1.333 + 0.5 = 1.833 A.
Equivalent of the two batteries alone. Veq = (5 + 6)/(1/3 + 1/2) = 11/0.8333 = 13.2 V, Req = 1/0.8333 = 1.2 Ω. Check with the 6 Ω load: 13.2/(1.2 + 6) = 1.833 A, load voltage 11 V.

answer.text: (b) Source in branch 1. Reduce from the far end:
Swapped: source in branch 2 (30 V in series with the 2 Ω), ammeter in branch 1 (in series with the 3 Ω):

answer: Reciprocity verified. The ammeter reads 2.222 A both times; the transfer conductance is 2.222/30 = 0.0741 S both ways. The source currents differ (5.062 A and 5 A), as expected: reciprocity says nothing about them.

Conditions. The ladder has one independent source, only resistors (linear, bilateral) and no dependent sources, and the ammeter is ideal, so reciprocity must hold. Adding a dependent source, or leaving a second source on, would break it.
Answer. (a) 11 V across the load; 1.333 A, 0.5 A and 1.833 A; equivalent 13.2 V behind 1.2 Ω. (b) 2.222 A in both positions.

bank.q: A 100 V RMS, 50 Hz source in series with 10 Ω feeds a 318.3 µF capacitor connected across the output terminals a-b. Find the Thevenin equivalent at a-b, the load that takes maximum average power (give its resistance and its inductance or capacitance), the maximum power, the current and voltage of that load, and the best purely resistive load with its power.
outline: Z<sub>th</sub> = 10 ∥ (−j10) = 5 − j5 Ω
Conjugate load 5 + j5 Ω: 5 Ω with 15.92 mH; P<sub>max</sub> = 250 W
Resistor only: R = |Z<sub>th</sub>| = 7.07 Ω, 207.1 W
answer: Capacitor reactance. XC = 1/(ωC) = 1/(2π × 50 × 318.3 × 10⁻⁶) = 1/0.1 = 10.0 Ω, so ZC = −j10 Ω.

answer.text: Thevenin voltage (open circuit, voltage division):
Thevenin impedance (source shorted: 10 Ω in parallel with −j10 Ω):

answer: Norton check. IN = Vth/Zth = (50 − j50)/(5 − j5) = 10 A, the current a short across a-b would draw: 100/10 = 10 A.
Best load. ZL = Zth* = 5 + j5 Ω: a 5 Ω resistor in series with an inductor of reactance 5 Ω, L = 5/(2π × 50) = 15.92 mH.

answer.text: Maximum power.
answer.pre:
P<sub>max</sub> = |V<sub>th</sub>|²/(4R<sub>th</sub>) = 70.71²/(4 × 5) = 5000/20 = 250 W
I = V<sub>th</sub>/(Z<sub>th</sub> + Z<sub>L</sub>) = (50 − j50)/10 = 5 − j5 A = 7.071∠−45° A
check: |I|²R<sub>L</sub> = 50 × 5 = 250 W   ✓
V<sub>L</sub> = I Z<sub>L</sub> = (5 − j5)(5 + j5) = 50 V = 50∠0° V

answer: The source then sees 10 Ω in series with the parallel pair, and the reactances cancel at the terminals: the total impedance seen by the Thevenin source is 10 Ω, purely resistive.

answer.text: Resistor-only load. With XL = 0, P = |Vth|²R/[(5 + R)² + 5²] is greatest at R = |Zth| = √(5² + 5²) = 7.071 Ω:
Comparison.

answer: Answer. Vth = 70.71∠−45° V, Zth = 5 − j5 Ω; the conjugate load 5 Ω with 15.92 mH takes 250 W; the best resistor, 7.071 Ω, takes 207.1 W.

bank.q: A 100 V RMS, 50 Hz source in series with 10 Ω has a capacitor of reactance −j10 Ω across its output terminals, and a load of 5 + j5 Ω is connected there. The load's inductive reactance then rises from 5 Ω to 8 Ω. Use the compensation theorem to find the new load current and power, and check by direct solution.
outline: Thevenin at the load: 50 − j50 V behind 5 − j5 Ω
Original I = 5 − j5 A (250 W)
V<sub>c</sub> = IΔZ = (5 − j5)(j3) = 15 + j15 V
ΔI = −V<sub>c</sub>/(Z<sub>th</sub> + Z<sub>L</sub> + ΔZ) = −1.789 − j0.963 A
answer: Thevenin equivalent seen by the load. Open circuit: Vth = 100(−j10)/(10 − j10) = 50 − j50 V. Source shorted: Zth = 10 ∥ (−j10) = 5 − j5 Ω.
The change. ΔZ = (5 + j8) − (5 + j5) = j3 Ω.

answer.text: Compensating source.

answer: Compensation network. Short the 100 V source, put the changed load 5 + j8 Ω in its branch with Vc in series, opposing I. The loop impedance is Zth + ZL + ΔZ = (5 − j5) + (5 + j8) = 10 + j3 Ω.

answer.text: Change in the load current.
New load current and power.
Direct check.

answer: Interpretation. The extra 3 Ω of reactance spoils the conjugate match: the reactances no longer cancel (net +j3 Ω in the loop), the current falls from 7.071 A to 6.773 A and the load power from 250 W to 229.4 W, a loss of 8.3 %. Because the power curve is flat near the match, a small drift costs little.
Other currents. The same compensating source, acting alone, gives the change in the capacitor and source currents too, by the current divider between the 10 Ω and the −j10 Ω.
Answer. The load current changes from 5 − j5 A to 3.211 − j5.963 A (6.773∠−61.7° A) and its power from 250 W to 229.4 W.

bank.q: For the ladder of the first question (a 20 V source, + at the top, in the left branch; 2 Ω, 6 Ω and 4 Ω along the top from left to right; 4 Ω and 3 Ω vertical resistors from the two inner top junctions to the bottom wire; a 10 V source, + at the top, in the right branch), compare mesh and nodal analysis: count the equations each needs, solve the circuit by nodal analysis, and show that it agrees with the mesh currents i₁ = 4 A, i₂ = 1 A, i₃ = −1 A. State in general when each method is the better choice.
outline: b = 7, n = 5: mesh needs 3 equations, nodal 4 − 2 = 2 (two nodes fixed by sources)
Nodal: v₂ = 12 V, v₃ = 6 V
Mesh currents recovered from node voltages
Effort comparison
General guidance: sources, counts, dependent sources, AC, simulators
answer: Counting. Branches: the two sources and five resistors, b = 7. Nodes: the bottom wire (reference) and four top junctions, n = 5. Mesh analysis needs b − n + 1 = 3 equations. Nodal analysis needs n − 1 = 4 unknowns, but the 20 V and 10 V sources each join a node to the reference, which fixes those node voltages: v₁ = 20 V (top of the 20 V source) and v₄ = 10 V (top of the 10 V source). Only v₂ (top of the 4 Ω) and v₃ (top of the 3 Ω) are unknown: 2 equations.

answer.text: Nodal equations (currents leaving each node):
Clear fractions (× 12 each):
Solve.
Agreement with the mesh currents.

head: Quantity
From node voltages
From mesh currents
rows: Top 4 Ω current, left to right

answer: Effort here. Nodal: 2 equations in 2 unknowns. Mesh: 3 equations in 3 unknowns (a 3 × 3 solution). Nodal is shorter for this ladder because both voltage sources are tied to the reference and remove unknowns for free.

When mesh analysis is better. Fewer meshes than independent nodes (long series chains); voltage sources that would otherwise make supernodes; current-controlled sources whose control current is a mesh current; when branch currents are the answer.

When nodal analysis is better. Fewer independent nodes than meshes (many parallel branches); current sources, which would otherwise make supermeshes; voltage-controlled sources; non-planar circuits, where windows do not exist; and large circuits, which is why simulators use modified nodal analysis.

Rule of thumb. Count b − n + 1 and n − 1, subtract one equation for each current source on an outside mesh branch (mesh) or each voltage source to the reference (nodal), and choose the smaller system. Both methods give the same answers, as the table shows, and both work for AC with impedances.
Answer. Mesh needs 3 equations and nodal 2; nodal gives v₂ = 12 V and v₃ = 6 V, which reproduce i₁ = 4 A, i₂ = 1 A and i₃ = −1 A.

bank.q: A 24 V battery feeds a workshop lamp through a long cable. With nothing connected the far end reads 24.0 V; with the lamp on it reads 23.0 V and the lamp draws 2.0 A. A 4 Ω heater is then switched on in parallel with the lamp. (a) Model the battery and cable by Thevenin's theorem. (b) Find the new lamp voltage and power, the heater power and the cable loss, assuming the lamp's resistance stays constant. (c) Would choosing the load for maximum power transfer be sensible here? (d) Evaluate replacing the cable by one with 0.2 Ω resistance.
outline: V<sub>th</sub> = 24 V, R<sub>th</sub> = (24 − 23)/2 = 0.5 Ω; lamp 11.5 Ω, 46 W
Lamp ∥ heater = 2.968 Ω; terminal voltage 20.54 V
Lamp 36.7 W (dims by 20 %), heater 105.5 W, cable 23.95 W, η = 85.6 %
Maximum power would need 0.5 Ω: 288 W at 50 % efficiency and 12 V
0.2 Ω cable: 22.48 V, lamp 43.96 W
answer: (a) Thevenin model. The open-circuit reading is Vth = 24 V. Loaded, the terminal voltage obeys V = Vth − RthI, so Rth = (24 − 23)/2 = 0.5 Ω (battery and cable together). The lamp's resistance is 23/2 = 11.5 Ω and it takes 23 × 2 = 46 W.

answer.text: (b) Heater on. The load is now 11.5 Ω in parallel with 4 Ω:
Powers.

answer: Check: 36.7 + 105.5 + 23.95 = 166.1 W. The lamp's power falls by about 20 %, which is the dimming seen. A real filament cools and its resistance falls a little, so the true dip is slightly smaller; the linear model is a good first estimate.

(c) Maximum power transfer? The theorem says the load would take the most power at RL = Rth = 0.5 Ω: 24²/(4 × 0.5) = 288 W, but only at 12 V across the load and with another 288 W heating the battery and cable (50 % efficiency). Lamps and heaters are made for a fixed voltage, not a fixed source, so the aim is to keep the terminal voltage near 24 V, which means RL much larger than Rth. Maximum power transfer is the wrong criterion for supplying power; it suits weak-signal sources.

answer.text: (d) Thicker cable, Rth = 0.2 Ω.

answer: With the heater on, the lamp now gets 44 W instead of 36.7 W, only 4.4 % below its 46 W, so the dimming is hardly visible, and the heater gives 126 W instead of 105 W. The cost is a heavier, dearer cable. The alternative, a separate cable for the heater, removes the shared R<sub>th</sub> entirely.

Evaluation. Thevenin's theorem turned two meter readings into a model that predicts every load. The fix is to reduce Rth (thicker or shorter cable, separate circuits), which raises efficiency and terminal voltage together; maximising power transfer would do the opposite.
Answer. Rth = 0.5 Ω; with the heater the lamp gets 20.54 V and 36.7 W; maximum power transfer is not sensible; a 0.2 Ω cable restores 22.48 V and 44 W.

glossary.def: A single two-terminal element, or elements in series carrying one current, between two nodes.
A point where two or more branches meet.
Any closed path through a circuit; a mesh is a loop with no other loop inside it.
A circuit that can be drawn on a flat sheet with no branch crossing another.
A current assigned to circulate round one mesh, used as the unknown in mesh analysis.
Two meshes treated together because a current source sits on their shared branch.
The node chosen as 0 V; every node voltage is measured from it.
Two non-reference nodes and the voltage source between them, treated as one node for KCL.
G = 1/R, in siemens (S).
A voltage or current source whose value is set by a voltage or current elsewhere in the circuit; never switched off in a theorem.
Scaling every source by k scales every response by k.
The response to several sources together is the sum of the responses to each alone.
An element that behaves the same for either direction of current, such as R, L or C.
The voltage across two terminals with nothing connected; equal to V<sub>th</sub>.
The current through a wire joining two terminals; equal to I<sub>N</sub>.
Replacing a voltage source V in series with R by a current source V/R in parallel with R, or the reverse.
Assume 1 A or 1 V at the far end of a ladder, work back to the source, then scale by homogeneity.
Current in one branch divided by the source voltage in another; equal both ways in a reciprocal network.
A branch with known voltage (or current) can be replaced by a source of that voltage (or current) without changing the rest of the network.
The voltage source V<sub>c</sub> = IΔZ that stands for a change ΔZ in a branch carrying I.
A complex number giving the RMS size and the phase of a sinusoid at one frequency.
Z = V/I for phasors, Z = R + jX in ohms.
Y = 1/Z in siemens; used for nodal analysis and Millman's theorem in AC.
A load Z<sub>L</sub> = Z<sub>th</sub>*, same resistance and opposite reactance, which takes the most average power.
Power reaching the load divided by the power the sources supply.
